title: IT Threat Intel - IT Cybersecurity
description: Curated IT / enterprise cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_threatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Brevo’s own embedded scripts were rewritten at the CDN edge to serve ClickFix lures and a WordPress backdoor — Sansec estimates more than 100,000 sites were exposed
items.content_text: Email-marketing platform Brevo, formerly Sendinblue, has confirmed a two-stage compromise that ended with its own customer-embedded scripts serving malware. On 14 September, between about 16:07 and 20:30 UTC, attackers used a long-lived Cloudflare API key with full account permissions that had been hardcoded in Brevo’s application source code to deploy a Cloudflare Worker that rewrote responses at the CDN edge. The Worker altered brevo.com, sendinblue.com, the login and account hosts and sibforms.com form hosting. It also altered the forms, Conversations chat widget and SDK loader scripts that customers embed in their own sites, and it stripped Content-Security-Policy headers along the way. Ordinary visitors to those sites were shown a fake “Cloudflare, verify you are human” ClickFix page telling them to paste and run a command. For visitors logged in as WordPress administrators, the script tried to install a malicious plugin, “Web Media Optimizer”, as a persistent backdoor with a hardcoded authentication bypass. Sansec, which first reported the attack, estimates that more than 100,000 websites were likely exposed; Brevo has not published its own count. Brevo says the key was first misused in late August, but it found no injection into customer-facing pages before 14 September. Its origin servers were never modified, and because the change happened at the edge, “standard integrity checks did not detect the change”. The first stage, on 10 September, was separate. An improperly scoped SAML single sign-on path gave the attacker access to 138 Brevo customer accounts; contacts were exported from 43 of them and phishing was sent from six. This story leads the edition ahead of Cisco’s exploited ISE zero-day because it is a confirmed compromise rather than a vulnerability, and because it reached every organisation that pasted a vendor’s script tag into its site: retailers, charities, schools and law firms alike. Brevo has revoked the key, removed the hardcoded credentials, deleted the attacker’s hostnames and purged its edge caches. It cannot clean the WordPress sites that received the plugin, or the computers of visitors who ran the command.

_threatfeed.source_name: Brevo incident write-up; Sansec; BleepingComputer; SecurityWeek

items.title: Gyazo lost 23.6 million user records and 490 million image-metadata records through its upload server — including session IDs, X integration tokens and text read from users’ screenshots
items.content_text: Helpfeel, the Japanese company behind the screenshot-sharing service Gyazo, has disclosed that an attacker exploited a flaw in its image upload server on 11 September and was removed on the 12th. The attacker took about 23.62 million user records, including anonymous accounts with no email address, plus about 490 million image-metadata records and a list of private images. The user fields include names or nicknames, email addresses, password hashes, user and device IDs, login session IDs, X (Twitter) integration tokens, Google sign-in emails and subscription status. The image metadata includes upload IP addresses, user agents, EXIF location data, titles, hashed passphrases and text extracted from screenshots by OCR. Payment card data was not affected. Helpfeel says it is still working out how many individuals are affected; it took the service offline, fixed the flaw, contacted the authorities and notified users. For an enterprise, the OCR text is a bigger concern than the account data. Screenshot tools tend to be installed informally, and people use them to capture dashboards, error messages, configuration pages and chat threads. Any credential, internal hostname or customer detail that appeared in a Gyazo screenshot may now sit as searchable text in the attacker’s copy.

_threatfeed.source_name: Helpfeel notice; SecurityWeek; BleepingComputer
_threatfeed.date_note: Intrusion 11 Sep 2026; disclosed 16 Sep 2026; reported 18 Sep 2026

items.title: A May npm-worm infection on a developer’s machine surfaced in September as a public leak of CrowdSec’s private repositories
items.content_text: CrowdSec, the open-source intrusion-prevention company, has traced a leak of its private source code back to the TanStack npm compromise of 11 May 2026. In that attack, TeamPCP pushed 84 malicious versions across 42 packages (CVE-2026-45321) carrying the “Shai-Hulud” credential-harvesting malware. The machine of a departed CrowdSec developer was infected, which exposed a GitHub OAuth token. On 22 May, in nine minutes between 05:52 and 06:01 UTC, about 170 private repositories were downloaded. The access was removed on 25 May, and someone tried to misuse an exposed AWS SNS credential on 17 August. On 16 September an archive appeared on an online forum containing more than 130 repositories, including console and SaaS code, data-science models and deployment scripts. It also held 83 user email addresses and the names and emails of 51 potential investors from 2020. CrowdSec says no client data was exposed, no infrastructure or databases were compromised and no production code was altered. It rotated credentials on 16–17 September with GitHub’s help. The timeline is the lesson. A developer-tool supply-chain infection in May became a public leak four months later, through a token that was still valid after the developer had left.

_threatfeed.source_name: CrowdSec; The Hacker News

items.title: Have I Been Pwned has independently verified 6.4 million people in the McKesson data — the 284 million the extortion group claims remains a claim
items.content_text: McKesson, one of the largest pharmaceutical and medical-supply distributors in the United States, confirmed at the end of August that an attacker had gained unauthorised access to third-party applications tied to its Oncology & Multispecialty and Medical-Surgical business units. The extortion group ShinyHunters demanded roughly $55 million by 1 September, McKesson did not pay, and the data was published. The number that matters arrived on 10 September and it came from neither side: Have I Been Pwned analysed the leaked dataset independently and verified approximately 6.4 million affected individuals, with names, addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers, employer details and health information among the exposed fields. ShinyHunters claims 284 million records. HIBP could not substantiate that figure, and could not substantiate the Social Security numbers the group also claimed to hold. Both numbers belong on the page, because the distance between them is the lesson: an extortion group’s stated record count is a negotiating position, routinely inflated by counting rows, duplicates and unrelated files rather than people, and it is the number that reaches the headlines first. The verified 6.4 million is the figure to plan against, and it is serious enough without help. McKesson says core distribution services remain operational and is offering credit monitoring to those affected.

_threatfeed.source_name: McKesson; Have I Been Pwned; SecurityWeek; The Register; HIPAA Journal
_threatfeed.date_note: Breach disclosed 31 Aug 2026; scope independently verified 10 Sep 2026

items.title: Revolut was tricked into handing over identity documents and full transaction history by an attacker impersonating a government agency — no software flaw was involved
items.content_text: Revolut disclosed on 14 September that an unauthorised party impersonated a government agency and, using what the company describes as valid technical domain credentials, submitted fraudulent data requests that its process treated as legitimate. The exposed fields for the affected subset of customers are unusually complete: names, addresses, dates of birth, copies of driving licences and passports, identity-verification selfies, IBANs, account statements and full transaction history including cryptocurrency activity. Revolut says customer funds and core systems were not affected, has blocked the attacker’s email, and has notified law enforcement, data-protection authorities and financial regulators while contacting affected users directly. The number of people affected has not been disclosed. Update, 17–18 September: SecurityWeek and American Banker have reported the scale and the route in, drawing on Hudson Rock and other investigators rather than on Revolut. They put the affected group at about 680 high-value customers, none of them in the US. The forged requests ran for five to six months from an Italian Ministry of the Interior certified-email (PEC) account compromised by infostealer malware, and went to Revolut Bank UAB in Lithuania. An actor calling itself “IAmNotAVillain” posted a US$3 million demand on 16 September. Revolut says it has received no direct contact or demand, and still describes the affected group only as “a limited number of customers”. What makes this worth the space on an all-IT page is that there is nothing to patch. The compromised control was an authorisation decision inside a legal-request workflow — a queue where the operating assumption is that the requester is who the letterhead says, and where refusing or delaying feels like obstructing an investigation. Any organisation with a channel through which police, regulators or government agencies can lawfully demand customer data has the same queue, usually staffed by a small team under time pressure, and usually without the verification step that would have stopped this.

_threatfeed.source_name: Revolut; SecurityWeek; American Banker; Infosecurity Magazine; The Record
_threatfeed.date_note: Disclosed 14 Sep 2026; scale and vector reported 17–18 Sep 2026

items.title: CenterPoint Energy confirms customer data was taken through an external-facing system — the 7.49 million record count is the attacker’s claim, and electric and gas delivery were not affected
items.content_text: Houston-based CenterPoint Energy, which serves about 7 million customers across Texas, Indiana, Minnesota and Ohio, said in an SEC 8-K filed on 14 September under Item 8.01 (other events), not Item 1.05, the item for material cybersecurity incidents, that an unauthorised third party obtained customer personal information through one of its external-facing systems. The company learned of it after someone posted online claiming to hold the data. It confirms that names, account information, billing information and the last four digits of Social Security numbers were taken for a portion of customers, says electric and gas delivery has not been impacted, and does not expect a material financial impact; outside experts are engaged and law enforcement and regulators have been notified. An actor claims to have pulled about 7.49 million records by abusing a public API with no rate limiting and has leaked a 2.5 GB archive. Neither CenterPoint nor the outlets reporting it have verified that count, and BleepingComputer puts the intrusion window at roughly 17 August to 1 September. The actor also threatened to go after the company’s “main infrastructure” next time; that is an unverified threat, and nothing reported so far indicates any operational impact. The lesson for enterprise IT is the entry point: a customer-facing interface that answered too many questions, too quickly, for too long without anyone noticing.

_threatfeed.source_name: CenterPoint Energy SEC 8-K; BleepingComputer; The Record; SecurityWeek

items.title: A trusted plugin update was the attack: Admin Menu Editor Pro’s own update server shipped a backdoor — the vendor counts about 230 customers affected and 300 more possibly, and a clean 2.37 is out
items.content_text: An attacker gained access to the server hosting adminmenueditor.com and used the premium WordPress plugin’s normal update mechanism to push a malicious version 2.35 of Admin Menu Editor Pro between roughly 06:00 and 13:00 UTC on 14 September. The replacement, version 2.36, was also compromised later the same day. The developer confirmed the incident in a notice on the vendor site. It now counts about 230 customers affected in the initial compromise and about 300 more possibly affected, depending on when they downloaded. Those figures are customers, meaning licences, not sites; the “1,500 sites” figure in early coverage came from BleepingComputer, not the vendor. The vendor says the attacker may have obtained root-level access to the distribution server, and on 19 September it released a clean version 2.37, built from 2.34. The backdoor drops a web shell at includes/wp-user-consent.php, creates a /wp-content/object-cache/ directory and wp_ocache* database options, and adds a hidden administrator account whose name begins with wp_. The vendor’s fuller list adds a cron hook _wp_cconsent_tick, a plugin named wordpress-cache-optimizer and a user wpsecuresuppbot. Version 2.34 is confirmed clean. There is no CVE, because nothing in the plugin’s code was vulnerable: the distribution channel was the flaw, and every site that did the responsible thing and auto-updated received the payload first.

_threatfeed.source_name: Admin Menu Editor developer notice and incident post; BleepingComputer
_threatfeed.date_note: Compromise 14 Sep 2026; vendor counts and clean 2.37 on 19 Sep 2026

items.title: AWS says data held only in its Bahrain region cannot be recovered after drone strikes — a disaster-recovery lesson, not an intrusion
items.content_text: Amazon Web Services has told customers that its Bahrain region, me-south-1, is “unable to restore access to the resources and data hosted exclusively in this Region” after Iranian drone strikes, because the damage “exceeded what its redundancy design could withstand”. In the UAE region, me-central-1, one availability zone (mec1-az2) is a total loss and work to restore the other two continues; AWS says “two of our facilities were directly struck” there. In Bahrain, a nearby strike caused structural and power damage, and fire suppression caused water damage. The strikes began in early March, and a second Bahrain zone was disrupted in April, which took the region fully offline. AWS says most customers had already moved using backups. Its next updates are due in early 2027 for Bahrain and in the coming months for the UAE. This is not an intrusion. It is on this page because it tests an assumption many cloud architectures make without writing it down. Multi-AZ is not the same as multi-region, and a region is a physical place. Data that lived in only one region, with no cross-region or off-provider copy, is now gone.

_threatfeed.source_name: AWS Health Dashboard, via Help Net Security

items.title: Veradigm confirms a patient-data breach through a vendor’s stolen credentials and a customer-service API — and says the scope is small, while “The Gentlemen” claims 3.5 million records with SSNs
items.content_text: Healthcare technology company Veradigm disclosed in an SEC filing that an attacker used credentials compromised at a third-party vendor to reach a Veradigm customer-service API and copy patient data. Two accounts of the same incident are now on the record and they do not agree, so this card carries both rather than choosing. Veradigm confirms that a breach occurred, is notifying affected customers and offering credit monitoring, and describes the scope as limited to a “small number of customers” reached only through that one interface. The ransomware group “The Gentlemen” claims a far larger haul — 3.5 million patient records including names, Social Security numbers, addresses, email addresses, phone numbers and guarantor information, with clinical data reportedly not taken — and set a ransom deadline of 11 September 2026. The 3.5 million figure is unverified and comes from the extortion group alone; the breach itself is not in doubt. The transferable lesson is the vector rather than the count. The credentials were not Veradigm’s, the interface was a service API rather than a login page, and API access of this kind is frequently outside the MFA and conditional-access policy that covers interactive sign-in.

_threatfeed.source_name: Veradigm SEC filing; BleepingComputer; HIPAA Journal

items.title: IDScan.net has confirmed the breach it was being sued over — 153 million driving-licence scans plus ID cards, travel documents and medical cards, with the FBI investigating
items.content_text: This item has changed state. IDScan.net, the identity-verification vendor used by banks, car rental firms, retailers, cannabis dispensaries, gun shops and hospitality businesses to check government-issued ID, has confirmed unauthorised access to its cloud platform. The intrusion was discovered around 1 September and disclosed on 4 September; the exposure is put at more than 153 million driving-licence scans, along with roughly 10 million ID cards, 3 million travel documents and 579,000 medical cards. It was first surfaced by Brian Krebs after the data was advertised on a dark-web marketplace called “Nexus”, and the FBI is investigating. That moves it from the litigation reporting this page carried last week to a confirmed vendor breach at very large scale. The reason it belongs on an all-IT page rather than in a sector column is that almost nobody chose to hold this data themselves. Age and identity verification is being pushed into more consumer and workplace flows by regulation and by platform policy, and each requirement creates another vendor holding scanned government identity documents on behalf of businesses that never wanted a repository. That data is the most durable a person has — a licence number and a scanned document cannot be rotated the way a password can — and the notification obligation tends to follow the business that chose the vendor, not only the vendor.

_threatfeed.source_name: BleepingComputer; Krebs on Security
_threatfeed.date_note: Breach confirmed 10 Sep 2026; first reported ~1–4 Sep 2026

items.title: Attackers are planting a Linux rootkit on F5 BIG-IP APM appliances that hides a web shell in memory and leaves nothing on disk
items.content_text: Reporting on 8 September describes intrusions in which F5 BIG-IP Access Policy Manager devices were compromised and fitted with a Linux rootkit that hooks the loading of PHP files and injects a fileless web shell straight into memory. Because no malicious file is written to the appliance’s filesystem, the usual checks — comparing binaries, scanning for dropped scripts, reviewing modified timestamps — come back clean while the attacker retains interactive access. The placement is what makes this expensive. BIG-IP APM is the authentication and remote-access front door for a large share of enterprise and government networks, so a device in this state sits between your users and everything they reach, with visibility of the sessions and credentials passing through it. Treat an affected appliance as a credential-exposure event rather than a malware cleanup, and assume anything that authenticated through it during the compromise window needs rotating.

_threatfeed.source_name: BleepingComputer

items.title: A phishing-as-a-service platform called BigBear 2.0 bypassed MFA at 258 organisations and collected more than 5,000 Microsoft 365 logins
items.content_text: Researchers detailed a phishing-as-a-service operation, BigBear 2.0, that defeated multi-factor authentication at 258 organisations and harvested over 5,000 Microsoft 365 credentials. The technique is adversary-in-the-middle: the victim reaches a proxy that relays the real Microsoft sign-in page, so the login looks correct, the MFA prompt is genuine and the user approves it — and the operator captures the resulting session token rather than the password. A stolen token is a working session, which is why resetting a password after this kind of compromise often changes nothing. Sold as a service, the platform puts this capability in reach of operators with no development ability of their own, which is how the victim count reaches the hundreds. The defensive answer is not more user training but authentication that cannot be relayed and session controls that notice when a token turns up somewhere implausible.

_threatfeed.source_name: BleepingComputer

items.title: Adobe has shipped an emergency fix for StyleSmuggler — CVE-2026-75650 is a CVSS 10.0 template-engine injection already used to backdoor Magento stores, and it is now in KEV
items.content_text: The zero-day Sansec named StyleSmuggler now has an identifier and a fix. Adobe issued an out-of-band update and confirmed exploitation against merchants, and CISA added CVE-2026-75650 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 8 September. The flaw is a template-engine injection carrying a maximum CVSS score of 10.0: attackers abuse Magento’s template system to inject PHP, triggering execution through the platform’s “Payment Transaction Failed Reminder” email path, and have used it to deploy a Rust backdoor and a PHP web shell. Sansec observed exploitation from 4 September, several days before the patch existed, which is the reason patching alone is not sufficient here. Any storefront that was internet-facing during that window should be treated as potentially backdoored until it has been checked — and that includes storefronts owned by marketing, run by an agency, or inherited with a subsidiary.

_threatfeed.source_name: CISA KEV catalog; Adobe security bulletin; Sansec advisory
_threatfeed.date_note: Exploitation observed from 4 Sep 2026; fixed and KEV-listed 8 Sep 2026

items.title: MikroTik routers are being taken over through exposed SSH — CERT Polska names the chain MikroTrick and gives you a one-line indicator to check for
items.content_text: CERT Polska warned that MikroTik RouterOS vulnerabilities are being actively exploited against devices with SSH reachable from the internet, with attacks occurring since at least 2 September 2026. Six issues were disclosed; the chain being used, which the CERT calls MikroTrick, combines CVE-2026-67276, an SSH authentication bypass rated CVSS 9.2, with CVE-2026-86060, an SSH privilege escalation through a crafted username also rated 9.2, to give an unauthenticated attacker full control of the device. A third flaw, CVE-2026-67277, is a memory disclosure issue in the bandwidth-test service rated 8.8. Fixes are in RouterOS 6.49.21, 7.23.4, 7.24.2 and 7.25beta3. The useful part of the advisory is the detection guidance: log entries showing a login failure for user “-2”, or an account added by ssh:-2@<ip>, indicate exploitation attempts, and the presence of a privileged account named “ops” indicates the device is already compromised. CERT Polska named 82.192.72.4 and 103.102.31.18 among the attacking sources. Cybernews reported roughly 122,500 exposed routers; patching alone does not evict an attacker who already has an account.

_threatfeed.source_name: CERT Polska advisory; BleepingComputer; The Hacker News; Cybernews
_threatfeed.date_note: Exploitation since at least 2 Sep 2026; reported 6–7 Sep 2026

items.title: Telus has told customers that attackers were logging into their accounts with valid credentials from February 2025 to June 2026 — sixteen months before disclosure
items.content_text: The Canadian telecommunications operator notified customers on 14 September of a campaign in which attackers used compromised credentials to sign into subscriber accounts and view or modify billing, subscription and contact details. In some cases they attempted to port service to a competing provider or altered subscriptions outright. Exposed data reported includes names, account numbers, phone numbers, billing addresses, partial card numbers and payment history. Telus has not disclosed how many accounts were affected, and has not said whether the credentials came from an internal compromise or from credential stuffing against reused passwords — a distinction that matters, because one is a breach of Telus and the other is a breach of its customers that Telus failed to absorb. The company has reset affected credentials, notified Vancouver Police and is offering identity-theft protection. The duration is the part worth studying: sixteen months of successful logins with valid credentials produced no detection, which is what account takeover looks like when monitoring is built around failed authentication rather than around the behaviour that follows a successful one. For enterprises the parallel is the customer or partner portal, which is usually the least-instrumented authentication surface in the estate.

_threatfeed.source_name: Telus; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Disclosed 14 Sep 2026; campaign ran Feb 2025 – Jun 2026

items.title: Florida’s driver database was accessed with credentials stolen from a law-enforcement officer’s personal device — no vulnerability was involved at any stage
items.content_text: Florida officials confirmed on 11 September that the state’s DAVID driver-record system was accessed using credentials taken from a law-enforcement officer’s personal device. There was no exploit, no unpatched server and no zero-day: the attacker logged in. Update, 16 September: ShinyHunters has published hundreds of thousands of the stolen files on its leak site, saying the state did not pay. TechCrunch reviewed a copy and describes vehicle ownership certificates carrying names, addresses and VINs, with Social Security numbers and non-US passports and immigration papers in a subset, and no driving-licence images or photos. The Record had already linked the intrusion to ShinyHunters, the same extortion group behind the McKesson breach above, which makes the week’s two largest identity-data incidents a matched pair driven by credentials rather than code. The state has not published a final affected-record count; credential revocation, a review of multi-factor authentication on law-enforcement data access and notification processes are under way. The uncomfortable structure here is one most enterprises share. A high-value data system is reachable by a population of privileged users who sit outside the organisation that owns the data, on devices that organisation does not manage, with an authentication decision it does not control. That describes a police officer and a state driver database; it equally describes a contractor, a franchisee, a distributor or a clinical partner reaching your customer or patient records from a laptop you have never inspected.

_threatfeed.source_name: Florida officials; TechCrunch; BleepingComputer; The Record

items.title: Seven agencies in four countries say North Korea’s WaterPlum infected more than 30,000 devices with fake job interviews — developers and IT staff are the target
items.content_text: Seven agencies in four countries issued a joint alert on 18 September about the North Korean group WaterPlum, also known as Contagious Interview: Japan’s National Police Agency and National Cybersecurity Office, the FBI, the US Defense Department’s Cyber Crime Center, Australia’s ACSC, and Germany’s BND and BfV. Between December 2025 and July 2026 the group infected at least 30,000 devices in more than 100 countries. It drained more than 7,000 cryptocurrency wallets of about ¥1.7 billion, roughly US$10.71 million. The method is the fake job interview. Operators pose as AI, cryptocurrency and NFT companies, or approach candidates through recruiting and freelance platforms, then ask applicants to download and run a project as a technical test. The projects deliver BeaverTail, InvisibleFerret, OtterCookie, OtterCandy and StoatWaffle; StoatWaffle runs through VS Code tasks. Japanese police and the FBI attribute WaterPlum, and some North Korean IT workers, to the 313 General Bureau of the Munitions Industry Department. The alert also covers the IT-worker scheme, which uses AI face-swapping and text-to-speech in video interviews and stolen identity documents to get real jobs. The targets are developers, engineers and IT staff, so the infected device can be a work machine, or a personal one that holds work credentials.

_threatfeed.source_name: FBI/IC3 joint alert; The Record; BleepingComputer

items.title: Spain’s data protection authority has received its first breach notification in which the attack was carried out by an AI agent — and the chain was ordinary
items.content_text: Spain’s data protection authority, the AEPD, says it has received its first personal-data breach notification involving an attack carried out with an autonomous AI agent. In the AEPD’s account, a third party used the agent “as an instrument”. The agent searched generic files for vulnerabilities, logged in with credentials it found there, located a flaw in an application, modified personal-data records and accessed invoices. The attacker used a well-known language model that the AEPD does not name, and the authority says this does not mean the model or its provider was compromised. The victim and its sector are not disclosed. Reports differ on how much a human directed each step, so the AEPD’s own wording is the safest guide. Deputy director Francisco Pérez Bes says one notification is not a trend, but it is a sign that AI-supported attacks “have ceased to be a theoretical risk”. Spain’s CCN has published guidance on offensive AI that covers faster patching, identity protection, supplier oversight and agent governance. The point to take away is how ordinary the chain is: found credentials, an application flaw and altered records. An agent simply does each step faster, and each step is covered by a control most organisations already have.

_threatfeed.source_name: AEPD; Help Net Security; Dark Reading

items.title: The GRIMWEDGE campaign chained two Chrome zero-days and a Windows ALPC bug through a compromised university website — the target was NGOs, the exposure is anyone running unpatched Chrome
items.content_text: Researchers disclosed on 15 September a campaign running since 1 September in which spear-phishing emails sent to non-governmental organisations linked to a compromised US university website, where a reflected cross-site-scripting flaw redirected visitors into a three-zero-day exploit chain. Two of the flaws are in Chrome — CVE-2026-85046 and CVE-2026-87491, the V8 and sandbox-escape bugs Google patched as its seventh in-the-wild zero-day of the year — and the third is CVE-2026-85880, the Windows ALPC elevation-of-privilege flaw that appeared in this month’s Patch Tuesday as an already-exploited zero-day. The chain delivers GRIMWEDGE, a multi-stage JavaScript backdoor capable of reconnaissance, file and process management and command execution, alongside a credential stealer tracked as LONGTALE. Attribution to the China-linked cluster UTA0560, overlapping with JungleBamboo and APT31, is researcher-assessed rather than official. The detail that generalises beyond the victims is the patch gap: fixes existed in the open-source Chromium code before they reached stable Chrome, and the attackers worked inside that interval. A browser is not patched because a fix has been committed, only because the build has shipped and the browser has been restarted.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News; Google Chrome release notes; Microsoft security bulletins

items.title: Red Heron automated a two-month-old Gitea exploit, scanned 1,386 instances and compromised 11 organisations — every victim was running a version patched in July
items.content_text: Researchers disclosed on 14 September that a group tracked as Red Heron built a public proof-of-concept for CVE-2026-60004, a critical remote code execution flaw in the self-hosted Gitea code platform, into a Python framework that registers its own accounts, exploits unpatched servers, steals repositories and cleans up behind itself. It scanned 1,386 Gitea instances across seven countries and Acronis, whose research team published the findings, confirmed compromises at 11 organisations in five countries — the United States, Taiwan, Canada, Argentina and Sri Lanka (some coverage gives 13 across six), spanning defence, elections, energy, aerospace, telecommunications and government. At one Taiwanese victim the group reached root on a three-node Proxmox cluster and deployed a custom Linux rootkit, SIXZUT, that patches fifteen kernel functions to hide its activity. Attribution to China is assessed at moderate confidence. The flaw was disclosed and fixed in July, which is the point worth carrying: this is not a zero-day campaign but an industrialised sweep of everyone who did not patch, and self-hosted developer tooling — stood up by a team, owned by nobody, absent from the asset register — is where that population concentrates.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News; researcher reporting

items.title: The FBI seized NightmareStresser, a DDoS-for-hire service linked to hundreds of thousands of attacks — the first visible disruption since the FBI’s new strategy
items.content_text: The FBI and the Department of Justice have seized nightmare-stresser[.]com and nightmarestresser[.]org, a DDoS-for-hire service, as part of the international Operation PowerOFF, which has run since December 2018. The service had been active since at least 2022 and is linked to hundreds of thousands of actual or attempted DDoS attacks worldwide. It had more than 566,000 registered users as of 2023, and ran on 52 dedicated servers offering Layer 4 and Layer 7 attacks of up to 200 Gbps. SecurityWeek describes it as one of the longest-running booter services. The sources read report no arrests. This is the first visible disruption since the FBI published its disruption-first cyber strategy on 10 September, which is covered under Regulation & Policy. The seizure takes down one storefront, not the demand behind it, so it changes nothing about your DDoS exposure this week. It does show the strategy turning into operations, and that is a reason to have a law-enforcement reporting route in place before you need it. Booter services sell Layer 7 floods as readily as volumetric ones, and those reach applications that network scrubbing alone does not protect.

_threatfeed.source_name: US Department of Justice and FBI; The Record; BleepingComputer; SecurityWeek

items.title: ShinyHunters defaced Clop’s leak site — the defacement is confirmed, but the claimed theft of Clop’s data and onion keys is not
items.content_text: The extortion group ShinyHunters, behind the McKesson and Florida DAVID incidents on this page, has defaced the Tor data-leak site of the Clop ransomware operation. BleepingComputer confirmed the defacement and an uploaded file reading “THIS SITE HAS BEEN PWN3D BY SHINYHUNTERES”. Everything else is ShinyHunters’ own claim, which BleepingComputer has not verified. The group says it got in through an unauthenticated file-upload flaw in the Grav CMS running the site. It also says it stole source code, plugins, system logs and the site’s onion-service private keys. ShinyHunters has given Clop 72 hours to make contact, and ties the feud to its allegation that Clop stole its Oracle E-Business Suite exploit in 2025. Clop has not responded. There is nothing for most defenders to do here, and the claims should be treated as claims. The story is carried as a signal about the ecosystem. The logs on a leak-site server can hold operator addresses and victim-negotiation traffic. If the key theft is real, Clop has lost control of its own identity on Tor. And one extortion crew publicly attacking another makes any data either group publishes less predictable.

_threatfeed.source_name: BleepingComputer; DataBreaches.net

items.title: Microsoft documented two access brokers phoning staff as the IT helpdesk, steering them onto personal devices, and then reading SharePoint and Exchange through the Graph API
items.content_text: Microsoft researchers detailed at least two initial-access-broker clusters, tracked as Storm-3032 and Storm-3121, running voice-phishing campaigns since May 2026. The call impersonates the internal IT helpdesk; the victim is directed to a convincing Microsoft sign-in page on a look-alike domain — the reported example pattern is of the form company.add-passkey.com — and crucially is steered to complete the step on a personal device. Credentials and session tokens are captured there, and the brokers then abuse the Microsoft Graph API to enumerate and exfiltrate data from SharePoint, OneDrive and Exchange in small, periodic transfers rather than one large pull. Access is reportedly sold on to extortion groups including ShinyHunters. Microsoft says it has not yet tied these campaigns to a confirmed corporate breach, so treat the technique as documented and the impact as unproven. The reason it earns a slot anyway is that every control most organisations rely on is bypassed by design: the phishing page is never opened on a managed endpoint, so EDR and conditional access see nothing; and the data movement happens through a first-party API that is indistinguishable from ordinary client traffic unless you are looking at volume and pattern.

_threatfeed.source_name: Microsoft threat research, via Dark Reading
_threatfeed.date_note: Reported 10 Sep 2026; campaigns observed since May 2026

items.title: Anthropic disclosed a fourth AI incident: during a January evaluation an early Claude Opus 4.6 build was told it was offline, was in fact on the live internet, and breached real third-party systems — undetected until August
items.content_text: Anthropic has disclosed that during a security evaluation in January 2026, an early version of Claude Opus 4.6 was told it was operating in an internet-isolated simulation but, because of a misconfiguration by evaluation partner Irregular, was actually connected to the live internet. The model went on to breach real third-party systems that it was unable to abort interacting with. The incident went undetected until August 2026. Anthropic has not named the affected organisations; following discovery it expanded its review to roughly 481 million transcripts and reports finding no other incident of comparable or greater severity. This is the fourth such incident tied to the same evaluation partner’s naming and configuration errors, and it is CONFIRMED by self-disclosure rather than by external investigation. It is carried here as a governance item, not an attack. The failure mode is one that any enterprise running agentic AI should recognise: the safety property was asserted in the prompt — the model was told it was isolated — rather than enforced at the network boundary, and the gap between the two was invisible for seven months because nobody was reconciling what the agent did against what the environment permitted.

_threatfeed.source_name: Anthropic disclosure; The Hacker News; Al Jazeera

items.title: Google’s threat intelligence group watched a criminal crew run a full credential-harvesting campaign in under six hours with an autonomous multi-agent framework
items.content_text: Google Threat Intelligence Group reported on 8 September that a financially motivated group executed a large-scale credential-harvesting campaign in less than six hours using an autonomous multi-agent framework — software agents handling the stages a team of operators would normally work through by hand. GTIG also observed actors going after proprietary AI models across healthcare, government and media, stealing API credentials and co-opting victim cloud environments to run their own AI workloads on someone else’s bill. GTIG’s John Hultquist put the takeaway bluntly: assume every threat actor is using AI in some capacity. For defenders, the useful reframing is about tempo rather than novelty. The tradecraft is familiar; what has changed is that a campaign which once took a week of operator effort now fits inside a single shift, which is shorter than most organisations’ detection and approval cycles.

_threatfeed.source_name: Google Threat Intelligence Group; The Hacker News

items.title: Attackers are phishing people into registering the attacker’s passkey on their Microsoft account — the mechanism sold as phishing-resistant, defeated by consent rather than by cryptography
items.content_text: Researchers described on 13 September two related campaigns against Microsoft 365 and cloud accounts. One is volume fraud: more than a million scam emails aimed at ACH and wire payment redirection. The second is the interesting one. Rather than trying to capture a credential or relay a token, the attacker walks the victim through registering an attacker-controlled passkey on the victim’s own account, using passkey-themed social engineering that borrows the language of a legitimate security upgrade. Nothing about the cryptography fails; the victim authorises the enrolment. The result is durable account access that survives a password reset and does not look like a compromise in the sign-in logs, because from the platform’s perspective the account simply has an additional valid authenticator. This does not make passkeys a bad control — they remain the strongest widely-available answer to credential phishing — but it moves the attack from the authentication event to the enrolment event, which is where most organisations have thought least.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News; researcher reporting

items.title: Cisco ISE has a CVSS 10.0 zero-day under active exploitation — unauthenticated root on the system that decides who gets onto your network, with no workaround
items.content_text: Cisco has confirmed active exploitation of CVE-2026-76460, a CVSS 10.0 flaw in Identity Services Engine that it describes as insufficient authentication control on an API endpoint. An unauthenticated remote attacker can bypass the web management interface and get root command execution. ISE and ISE-PIC 3.0 through 3.5 are affected. Fixes are in 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 P11, 3.3 P12, 3.4 P7 and 3.5 P4, and there is no workaround. CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 September with a three-day federal deadline of 19 September, now passed. No actor has been named, and Cisco warns that attackers may “remove or hide evidence of exploitation”. This is the third actively exploited ISE flaw since June 2025, after CVE-2025-20281 and CVE-2025-20337. It is also Cisco’s second exploited zero-day in a matter of days, after the Secure Email Gateway flaw below. The product’s role is why this ranks just behind the lead story. ISE is the policy engine that decides which users and devices get onto the wired, wireless and VPN network, and what they can reach once there. VulnCheck notes that root on ISE lets an attacker rewrite network access policy, pull stored credentials, delete logs and move laterally. The control meant to contain an intruder ends up working for the intruder.

_threatfeed.source_name: Cisco PSIRT; CISA KEV catalog; CyberScoop; The Hacker News; Help Net Security
_threatfeed.date_note: Advisory and KEV listing 16 Sep 2026; reported 17 Sep 2026

items.title: Cisco’s firewall-management console has three attack clusters on it — one Sandworm-linked by tooling, one that deployed Qilin — and the hardening release shipped on 16 September
items.content_text: Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center remains the clearest example this month of attackers going after the system that manages the perimeter. CVE-2026-20079 (CVSS 10.0) is an unauthenticated authentication bypass that gives root command execution through crafted HTTP requests; CVE-2026-20316 (CVSS 5.3) is a hardcoded low-privilege credential. Cisco Talos separates the activity into three clusters. UAT-12197, unattributed, uses CVE-2026-20079 to plant JSP web shells and a cmd.jar credential extractor. UAT-11823, which Talos tracks as an APT, chains both flaws and deployed a 64-bit Linux variant of Cyclops Blink, malware previously attributed to Sandworm. Talos says the cluster’s tooling overlaps with Sandworm’s, which makes it Sandworm-linked, not a Sandworm attribution. UAT-11988, assessed with high confidence as a ransomware operator whose tradecraft matches Qilin affiliates, entered through CVE-2026-20316 alone and deployed Qilin on selected endpoints. CISA added CVE-2026-20079 to KEV on 9 September with a 12 September deadline, now passed. Correction: the previous edition said CVE-2026-20316 had been in KEV since 29 July and was flagged for ransomware use. The KEV catalog has no entry for it; 29 July is when exploitation was first reported. Update, 16 September: Cisco published its September hardening advisory for ASA, FTD and FMC (cisco-sa-hardening-asaftdfmc-uvpPROhN). It covers eight CVEs found in internal review, CVE-2026-20329 to CVE-2026-20336, with fixed FTD and FMC releases 7.0.10, 7.2.12, 7.4.8, 7.6.6, 7.7.13, 10.0.2 and 10.1.0.

_threatfeed.source_name: Cisco PSIRT; Cisco Talos; CISA KEV catalog; BleepingComputer
_threatfeed.date_note: Talos report 9 Sep 2026; hardening release 16 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA added three Linux kernel flaws to KEV with a three-day deadline — nobody has said how they are being exploited, which is a reason to move faster, not slower
items.content_text: CISA added three Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 18 September with a federal deadline of 21 September. CVE-2025-39682 is in the kernel TLS receive path, where a zero-length record gets past record-type handling. The Hacker News gives it CVSS 9.8, and Red Hat cites known public exploits. CVE-2026-53266 is an out-of-bounds write in ebtables SNAT handling that leads to privilege escalation, rated CVSS 8.8. CVE-2025-39964 is a race condition in the AF_ALG crypto socket interface, rated CVSS 7.8. Red Hat has updated its advisories to acknowledge exploitation, but nobody has said who is exploiting the flaws, how, or whether they are being used together. CISA’s entries carry two notes worth reading closely: affected products may be end-of-life, and the vulnerable component can be embedded in other products. The second note is where most enterprises are exposed. General-purpose servers get kernel updates through the normal distribution channel, but appliances, network devices, hypervisor hosts and container platforms built on Linux often do not. Local privilege escalation also matters most on shared systems. On a container node, a CI runner or a multi-tenant server, anyone who can run code there counts as a local user.

_threatfeed.source_name: CISA KEV catalog; Red Hat; The Hacker News

items.title: Google says a Pixel cellular-modem flaw may be under limited, targeted exploitation — CISA gave federal agencies three days to patch their phones
items.content_text: Google’s September Pixel update fixes CVE-2026-58704, a logic error in the Pixel cellular modem that lets an attacker bypass permission checks and escalate privileges. It is rated CVSS 8.0, and Google says it “may be under limited, targeted exploitation”. The Hacker News describes it as zero-click, needing no user interaction. CISA added it to the KEV catalog on 16 September with a federal deadline of 19 September. Devices at security patch level 2026-09-05 or later are protected. Neither Google nor CISA has attributed the activity, and descriptions of it elsewhere as spyware tradecraft are not sourced to either. The same bulletin fixed 110 vulnerabilities, 46 of them critical. For an enterprise, the words “limited, targeted” are a reason to act, not a reason to relax. Baseband exploits are expensive, so they are used against a small set of people: executives, legal and deal teams, journalists, and staff who travel to high-risk jurisdictions. That group is usually easy to identify, and their phones often escape the patch discipline applied to laptops.

_threatfeed.source_name: Google Pixel security bulletin; CISA KEV catalog; The Hacker News

items.title: GitLab’s CVSS 10.0 path traversal reads any file on the server in one unauthenticated request — and went from disclosure to confirmed exploitation in three days
items.content_text: CVE-2026-85706 is an unauthenticated path traversal in the repository commits interface of self-managed GitLab: a single crafted HTTP request returns the contents of an arbitrary file from the server, with no credentials and no user interaction. GitLab disclosed and patched it on 11 September in 19.3.2, 19.2.6 and 19.1.8; affected versions run from 18.7 through 19.1.8, 19.2 through 19.2.6 and 19.3 through 19.3.2, and the instance needs at least one public project for the request to land. watchTowr Labs and CISA both reported internet-wide probing almost immediately, and on 14 September CISA and GitLab each confirmed exploitation in the wild; the flaw was added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 11 September with a federal civilian deadline of 14 September, now passed. On 16 September Hong Kong’s HKCERT also warned that the flaw is being exploited in the wild; no count of compromised instances has been published. GitLab.com SaaS customers were not affected. The reason this is worse than a file-read sounds is what a GitLab server keeps on disk. CI/CD variables, runner registration tokens, deploy keys, integration secrets and database credentials all live there, so an arbitrary read is a credential harvest against every pipeline the instance runs — and those credentials keep working after the patch is applied.

_threatfeed.source_name: GitLab advisory; CISA KEV catalog; watchTowr Labs; HKCERT; BleepingComputer; Cybersecurity Dive; Dark Reading
_threatfeed.date_note: Disclosed and patched 11 Sep 2026; exploitation confirmed 14 Sep 2026

items.title: A ScreenConnect authorisation flaw is being used to push payloads between connected machines — CISA gave federal agencies three days to patch it
items.content_text: CVE-2026-84869 is a missing-authorisation and improper-privilege-management flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect, rated CVSS 9.9 and confirmed exploited. Attackers abuse legitimate remote-support sessions to transfer and execute files without the host confirming the transfer, then use social engineering to get a victim to run a modified ScreenConnect client that detects active sessions and propagates VBScript payloads to the machines on the other end of them. That is the worm-like behaviour in the reporting: not a self-replicating network worm, but spread along established trust relationships between a support console and the endpoints it already reaches. Exploitation has been reported since 20 August. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 11 September and, under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, gave federal agencies three days to remediate — an unusually compressed clock that is itself a signal about observed activity. ConnectWise fixed it in version 26.6.5, with disabling the TransferFiles permission offered as an interim mitigation. For anyone whose IT is delivered by a managed service provider, the relevant instance may not be one you administer, and the blast radius runs from that provider outward through every client it supports.

_threatfeed.source_name: ConnectWise advisory; CISA KEV catalog; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: KEV-listed 11 Sep 2026; exploitation reported from 20 Aug 2026

items.title: A crafted email is enough to get root on a Cisco Secure Email Gateway — CVE-2026-76461 is under active exploitation and there is no workaround
items.content_text: Cisco has confirmed active exploitation of CVE-2026-76461, a CVSS 9.8 flaw in Cisco AsyncOS for Secure Email Gateway, physical and virtual, that lets an unauthenticated remote attacker run arbitrary commands with root privileges on the underlying operating system. Reporting describes the path as SQL injection reached through the appliance’s parsing of an inbound message, which is the uncomfortable part: the attack vector is the product doing its job. No user has to click anything, no management interface has to be exposed, and no credential is needed — the gateway accepts hostile input from the internet by design, and that is the input. All configurations are affected and Cisco states there is no workaround; fixes are in AsyncOS 15.5.5-0141, 16.0.4-302 and 16.5.0-780, shipped alongside a security-hardening advisory. Secure Email and Web Manager and Secure Web Appliance are not affected. Cisco says multiple customers were likely compromised before disclosure and has contacted affected Secure Email Cloud customers with indicators of compromise; attribution is unknown. CISA added the flaw to the KEV catalog on 14 September with a federal deadline of 17 September. Cisco Identity Services Engine has since followed with an exploited CVSS 10.0 zero-day (see above). That makes three Cisco enterprise products on this page under confirmed exploitation, alongside Secure Firewall Management Center, and all three share a shape: perimeter infrastructure that sees everything, trusted implicitly, and rarely covered by endpoint detection.

_threatfeed.source_name: Cisco PSIRT; CISA KEV catalog; SecurityWeek; The Hacker News; BleepingComputer
_threatfeed.date_note: Advisory and KEV listing 14 Sep 2026; reported 15 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA now marks the VMware vCenter RCE CVE-2026-59310 as used by ransomware — the flaw that was an espionage story in August is now an extortion one
items.content_text: CISA has updated its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities entry for CVE-2026-59310, a remote code execution flaw in VMware vCenter Server, to record known use in ransomware campaigns, as reported by BleepingComputer on 15 September. Broadcom patched the flaw on 29 July, and CISA added it to the catalog on 18 August with a federal deadline of 21 August. CISA has not named the ransomware groups involved or said how many organisations are affected. The earlier phase of exploitation is better documented: during mid-August APT activity, the DFIR firm QUIRSO counted 361 compromised IP addresses across 47 countries, and Shadowserver has tracked around 450 exposed vCenter servers. The change of status matters more than the change of wording. vCenter is the control plane for a virtualised estate, so an operator with code execution there can reach every guest it manages at once — which is exactly the position an encryption-focused crew wants, and exactly why a host that was quietly compromised in August may now be holding a second, less patient visitor.

_threatfeed.source_name: CISA KEV catalog; Broadcom; BleepingComputer; QUIRSO; Shadowserver
_threatfeed.date_note: KEV-listed 18 Aug 2026; ransomware use reported 15 Sep 2026

items.title: Microsoft ships the largest Patch Tuesday on record — around 974 CVEs, and two Windows zero-days are already being exploited
items.content_text: Microsoft’s September rollup is the largest it has ever shipped, and the vendor counts do not agree: Microsoft, Tenable and SecurityWeek put it at 974 CVEs, while BleepingComputer counts 966 Microsoft flaws and 999 once 25 third-party CVEs are folded in. More than 100 are rated critical. Two are already being exploited: CVE-2026-81963, a link-following elevation of privilege in the Windows Update Stack, and CVE-2026-85880, a heap-based buffer overflow in Windows ALPC. Both carry CVSS 7.8, both hand an attacker who already has a foothold full SYSTEM privileges, and CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day. The scale is the problem: a month’s worth of triage capacity will not stretch across a thousand identifiers, so the two exploited local-privilege bugs need to be pulled out and shipped first.

_threatfeed.source_name: Microsoft security updates; CISA KEV catalog; CyberScoop; BleepingComputer; SecurityWeek; Tenable

items.title: Microsoft has now shipped six emergency fixes for its own September update — KB5129195 restores Remote Desktop Services after the record Patch Tuesday broke it
items.content_text: Microsoft released out-of-band update KB5129195 on 14 September to fix RDP connections dropping after several minutes, sign-in failures and servers hanging at configuration prompts, with Microsoft Management Console and File Explorer also affected. It is the sixth emergency patch the company has shipped off the back of this month’s cumulative update — the 8 September Patch Tuesday, the largest on record at 966 to 974 CVEs, including two actively exploited Windows elevation-of-privilege zero-days, CVE-2026-81963 in the Update Stack and CVE-2026-85880 in ALPC. The operational risk now is not the regression itself but the conclusion people draw from it. Six emergency fixes in a week is a strong argument for waiting, and waiting means leaving unpatched two flaws that are already being used to reach SYSTEM — one of which, the ALPC bug, appears in the GRIMWEDGE espionage chain covered elsewhere on this page. The honest position is that this month’s update is both necessary and unusually disruptive, and the answer is sequencing and a pilot ring rather than deferral.

_threatfeed.source_name: Microsoft; Infosecurity Magazine
_threatfeed.date_note: Out-of-band update released 14 Sep 2026; reported 15 Sep 2026

items.title: Acronis says its cPanel & WHM backup plugin flaw CVE-2026-87886 has been used in limited, targeted attacks and is now in KEV — a root path on shared hosting servers
items.content_text: Acronis advisory SEC-10986 covers CVE-2026-87886, a Linux local privilege escalation caused by insecure file permissions in the Acronis Backup plugin for cPanel & WHM and the corresponding Plesk extension. It is low complexity but requires an authenticated local foothold. Acronis says it has seen exploitation in limited, targeted attacks against cPanel & WHM only, based on a report from a potentially affected customer. Fixes are in cPanel & WHM plugin 1.9.3 HF3 and Plesk extension 1.8.11. CISA added it to the KEV catalog on 16 September with a federal deadline of 19 September, now passed. The KEV entry covers both the cPanel & WHM plugin and the Plesk extension, although Acronis has reported exploitation against cPanel & WHM only. The scale is small, and the reason it is on this page is the setting: on a shared hosting server, an authenticated local user is simply a customer, or anyone who has compromised one customer’s site, so a privilege escalation in a backup plugin running on every tenant’s box is a route from one site to all of them.

_threatfeed.source_name: Acronis advisory SEC-10986; CISA KEV catalog; BleepingComputer; Help Net Security

items.title: Attackers are uploading PHP web shells to WooCommerce stores through a lead-capture plugin patched in February — Wordfence has blocked more than 100,000 attempts
items.content_text: Wordfence has blocked more than 100,000 attempts to exploit CVE-2026-27540, an unauthenticated arbitrary file upload flaw in the Wholesale Lead Capture plugin for WooCommerce. The plugin’s AJAX upload handler, wwlc_file_upload_handler, does not validate file types, so an anonymous visitor can upload a PHP web shell. Wordfence rates the flaw CVSS 9.8. The shell.php that attackers drop reports host details and provides an upload form for writing more files. Versions up to 2.0.3.1 are affected. The fix, 2.0.3.2, shipped on 20 February 2026, so every site being hit now has gone seven months without applying it. Activity peaked between 4 and 17 June, with further spikes on 1 July and 30 August. The plugin has only about 6,000 active installations, but they are B2B and wholesale storefronts: sites that take trade-account registrations and payments, where a web shell is a short step from card skimming or customer-data theft. It is not in KEV. The pattern matters more than the plugin. Attackers keep scanning for months-old flaws in niche commerce plugins because small stores patch late.

_threatfeed.source_name: Wordfence; BleepingComputer; The Hacker News; Infosecurity Magazine

items.title: CISA added four exploited flaws to KEV on 8 September — two Windows zero-days, the Adobe Commerce zero-day, and a CVSS 10.0 pre-auth RCE in N-able N-central
items.content_text: All four entries in CISA’s 8 September batch have vendor patches available, so this is a scheduling problem rather than a research one. Two are the Windows zero-days from the same day’s Patch Tuesday: CVE-2026-81963 in the Windows Update Stack and CVE-2026-85880 in Windows ALPC, both CVSS 7.8 and both granting SYSTEM. The third is CVE-2026-75650, the Adobe Commerce and Magento template-engine injection rated CVSS 10.0 that Adobe fixed out of band. The fourth is CVE-2026-86218, a static code injection giving pre-authentication remote code execution in N-able N-central, also CVSS 10.0, with a federal civilian remediation deadline of 11 September. Read as a set, the batch says something useful about where attackers are working: local privilege escalation on Windows endpoints, internet-facing commerce platforms, and the management tooling that reaches everything else.

_threatfeed.source_name: CISA KEV catalog

items.title: CISA’s 9–10 September KEV additions put Cisco, Citrix and Fortinet on a 12 September clock — and record ransomware operators exploiting WatchGuard Firebox
items.content_text: Three actively exploited flaws went into the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog in the same bundle with a 12 September federal remediation deadline, now passed: Cisco’s Secure Firewall Management Center bypass CVE-2026-20079 at CVSS 10.0, covered in its own card above, where Cisco Talos separates the activity into three clusters, including one whose tooling overlaps with Sandworm and a ransomware operator that entered through the companion flaw CVE-2026-20316 and deployed Qilin; a Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway authentication bypass, CVE-2026-19490, at CVSS 9.3, with 56 exploitation attempts documented since early September; and Fortinet’s CVE-2025-25249 in FortiOS, FortiSwitchManager and FortiSASE, rated around 7.3, now weaponised to deliver a remote access trojan tracked as PivotC2 — more than 3,000 IP addresses targeted, with at least 178 devices compromised, most of them in the United States, by suspected Russian-speaking actors. Separately, on 10 September CISA updated its existing KEV entry for CVE-2025-14733 in WatchGuard Firebox to record that ransomware operators are now exploiting it. WatchGuard patched that flaw in December 2025 and close to 9,000 devices were still unpatched and internet-exposed as of 8 September. Read alongside the SonicWall SMA1000 pair and the N-able N-central entry from the previous week, the whole internet-facing appliance category is being worked through inside a fortnight. Every one of these has a vendor fix already available, which makes the constraint scheduling and ownership rather than research.

_threatfeed.source_name: CISA KEV catalog; The Hacker News; SecurityWeek; BleepingComputer

items.title: Three JFrog Artifactory flaws chain from anonymous token to administrator in under five minutes — and researchers put half of internet-reachable instances still at risk
items.content_text: Attackers are chaining CVE-2026-42018, a token-disclosure flaw rated CVSS 7.5 that yields an internal anonymous-user JWT even where anonymous access is disabled, with CVE-2026-42016, an insufficient token-validation issue rated CVSS 8.1 that escalates that token to administrator — in some observed cases in under five minutes — before deploying a custom Rust-based command-and-control backdoor. A third flaw, CVE-2026-82329, is a critical authentication bypass in the same product. Attacks were reported publicly from 11 September; Wiz’s timeline puts exploitation of the first two back to 15 August. CISA added those two to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 11 September with a federal deadline of 25 September, still open. JFrog has fixed them in 7.111.21 and later, depending on branch. Researchers estimate that between 49% and 62% of internet-reachable Artifactory instances remain vulnerable to at least one of the three. Update, 17 September: Wiz has documented six malicious Groovy user plugins dropped into $JFROG_HOME/var/etc/artifactory/plugins/. They include command shells, a dumper for decrypted LDAP, Crowd and proxy secrets, token tables and signing material, and a memory-resident Tomcat filter backdoor triggered by an X-Request-Trace header. The plugins survive patching and reload on restart, so upgrading closes the way in but leaves the backdoor in place. The severity is not really the CVSS scores, which are moderate individually; it is the position of the product. An artifact registry is the thing your builds trust without checking, so administrator access to it is administrator access to everything compiled, containerised or deployed from it afterwards.

_threatfeed.source_name: JFrog advisory; CISA KEV catalog; Wiz; BleepingComputer; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Attacks reported 11 Sep 2026; KEV-listed 11 Sep 2026; Wiz persistence update 17 Sep 2026

items.title: Check Point’s management and log servers have an unauthenticated root flaw triggered by an over-long username — no exploitation yet, and LivePatch fixes it
items.content_text: Check Point has disclosed CVE-2026-91843, a stack overflow in the login process of its Quantum Security Management Server, Log Server and Multi-Domain Server. A login request with a very long username gives an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution as root, and the flaw is rated CVSS 9.8. Self-managed and standalone deployments are affected; Smart-1 Cloud is not. Vulnerable builds include R82.10 at Jumbo Hotfix Take 44 or below, R82 at Take 126 or below, R81.20 at Take 166 or below and R81.10 at Take 190 or below. The Hacker News reports that every R82.20 build is affected and that no protective Jumbo Hotfix was yet available for it. End-of-support R81 and R80.x are also vulnerable. The fix is delivered through LivePatch (sk1000155). There is no indication of exploitation and the flaw is not in KEV; Check Point has published detection guidance and indicators. Censys sees about 3,836 hosts exposing the management service’s identity, which counts product presence, not confirmed-vulnerable systems. A management server holds the policy for every gateway beneath it. This disclosure also follows the Dutch NCSC’s warning that exploitation of Check Point’s VPN flaws is imminent, so attackers are watching this vendor closely. The time to close it is before a proof of concept appears.

_threatfeed.source_name: Check Point advisory; BleepingComputer; The Hacker News; Censys

items.title: The Dutch NCSC calls exploitation of two Check Point VPN flaws imminent — there is still no confirmed in-the-wild activity, and that gap is the whole opportunity
items.content_text: The Netherlands’ national cyber security centre issued a warning on 12 September that exploitation of two Check Point vulnerabilities is imminent, rating both likelihood and impact as high. CVE-2026-85102 is an improper certificate-validation flaw during VPN negotiation and CVE-2026-85103 is a heap overflow in the VPN certificate decoder; both can lead to remote code execution on Security Gateways and Management Servers. Check Point released fixes on 9 September through LivePatch Take 24 and its Jumbo Hotfix Accumulators, covering the R81.x and R82.x lines plus several end-of-support versions, with R82.20 unaffected. Two things should be stated plainly, because the headline word is “imminent”: there is no confirmed exploitation in the wild and no public proof-of-concept reported at the time of writing, and the flaws are not in the KEV catalog. The NCSC is forecasting from a pattern — the speed with which VPN and remote-access flaws have been weaponised across vendors this year — not reporting an observation. That makes this the one item on the page you can still get ahead of, and the certificate-handling code is reached during negotiation, before any user authenticates. As of 18 September, BleepingComputer still reported no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation. A separate unauthenticated root flaw in Check Point’s management and log servers, CVE-2026-91843, was disclosed on 16 September and has its own card.

_threatfeed.source_name: Dutch NCSC; Check Point advisory; BleepingComputer
_threatfeed.date_note: NCSC warning 12 Sep 2026; vendor fixes released 9 Sep 2026

items.title: SAP’s September update fixes a maximum-severity kernel flaw, OVERPASS, that allows unauthenticated remote command execution
items.content_text: SAP’s September patch day covers 20 flaws, headlined by a maximum-severity memory corruption bug in the SAP Kernel — named OVERPASS — in the handling of Extended Passport data. Successful exploitation allows an unauthenticated attacker to run commands remotely, recover secrets and modify data. No exploitation has been reported and patches are available, which puts this firmly in the plan-and-schedule category rather than the emergency one. The reason it still deserves attention is what SAP systems hold: the kernel sits beneath the ERP applications that run finance, procurement and supply-chain operations, so the blast radius of a compromise is the business rather than a server. SAP patching is also usually slow by design, tied to release windows and application-team sign-off, so the useful action this week is booking the change rather than debating the severity.

_threatfeed.source_name: SAP security notes; BleepingComputer

items.title: A FreeIPA flaw chain lets a client that never authenticated create a Kerberos identity and add itself to the administrators group
items.content_text: Red Hat disclosed on 8 September that a chain of flaws in FreeIPA allows an entirely unauthenticated client to create a Kerberos identity of its choosing and place that identity in the administrators group. The chain abuses an access-control rule intended to let users manage their own one-time-password tokens, and it requires a second flaw in 389 Directory Server to complete. The FreeIPA half is CVE-2026-76578, rated critical with a preliminary CVSS of 9.8, and Red Hat says it reproduced the attack twice against a default installation — meaning no unusual configuration is needed. A fix is available in FreeIPA 4.13.4, and Red Hat ships the same technology as Identity Management. No exploitation has been reported. The severity comes from what FreeIPA is: if it is your identity source for Linux estates, this is a direct route to domain-wide administrative control.

_threatfeed.source_name: Red Hat; The Hacker News

items.title: Google patched the seventh Chrome zero-day of 2026 — and four separate espionage groups were already running the same exploit kit that uses it
items.content_text: Google released a Chrome update on 9 September fixing CVE-2026-87491, an out-of-bounds write in V8, the browser’s JavaScript and WebAssembly engine, and confirmed the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A crafted HTML page is enough to execute code inside the renderer sandbox. The fixed builds are 153.0.8010.36 and .37. This is the seventh actively exploited Chrome zero-day Google has patched in 2026, and it arrives five days after the sixth, CVE-2026-85046, which is also still worth confirming across your fleet. What makes it more than a routine browser patch is who was already using it: researchers found four distinct nation-state-linked groups, one of them APT31 from 28 August, running the same exploit kit — tracked as BlueMoon — chaining CVE-2026-85046 and CVE-2026-87491 inside a single week. Four unrelated actors converging on one chain that fast points at a shared exploit broker rather than four independent discoveries. Two practical notes decide whether you are actually protected. Chrome applies its update on restart, so a fleet where nobody closes the browser is a fleet that is not patched. And every Chromium-based browser in the estate inherits this: Edge, Brave, Opera, Vivaldi and any embedded Electron application ship their own V8 and need their own updates on their own vendor schedules.

_threatfeed.source_name: Google Chrome release blog; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Patched 9 Sep 2026; BlueMoon research published 9 Sep 2026

items.title: The N-able N-central pre-auth RCE is now confirmed exploited and in KEV — CVSS 10.0, with a federal deadline of 11 September
items.content_text: The exploitation status of CVE-2026-86218 changed on 8 September: N-able confirmed exploitation in the wild, and CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog with a federal civilian remediation deadline of 11 September. The flaw is a static code injection in N-central giving pre-authentication remote code execution, rated CVSS 10.0. N-able shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — its fourth hotfix for this product in five weeks. Two further high-severity issues, CVE-2026-86206 and CVE-2026-86207, were addressed alongside it. Huntress reported attacks against N-central’s API and appliance logs from 4 September. N-central is a remote monitoring and management platform holding privileged agents on every endpoint it manages, so compromising the server means compromising everything below it — and for a managed service provider, every client at once.

_threatfeed.source_name: CISA KEV catalog; N-able advisory; Huntress
_threatfeed.date_note: Hotfix released 5 Sep 2026; exploitation confirmed and KEV-listed 8 Sep 2026

items.title: The PaperCut attacker scaled the campaign with hundreds of automated AI agents and has now compromised more than 440 instances
items.content_text: Attackers are chaining two flaws in PaperCut MF and NG — CVE-2026-81578, an access-control bypass, and CVE-2026-82078, unsafe dynamic class loading — into full compromise of a print server with nothing more than an IP address or hostname to start from. Huntress confirmed the first wave in late August against education, healthcare and construction organisations in the United States, Denmark and Ireland, with credential theft as the observed objective. The Hacker News reported on 10 September that the same actor then scaled the campaign using hundreds of automated AI agents, reaching more than 440 compromised instances across multiple countries. PaperCut shipped three emergency patches, the last on 1 September. Print servers are an unusually good place to harvest credentials from, for reasons that apply well beyond education: they are integrated with the directory so they can authenticate users and enforce quotas, they are reachable from across the whole internal network because everyone prints, and they are owned by whoever manages printing rather than by the team that patches servers.

_threatfeed.source_name: Huntress; PaperCut security bulletin; Cybersecurity Dive; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: First reported 31 Aug 2026; campaign scale updated 10 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA and NIST set concrete numbers for cloud identity tokens and signing keys — one-hour tokens, 90-day key rotation for high-impact systems, and no tokens in logs
items.content_text: CISA and NIST have co-authored NIST IR 8587, guidance on protecting the identity tokens and signing keys that cloud authentication depends on. The recommendations are specific. Access and identity tokens should be valid for at most one hour, and expired tokens should be rejected outright. Signing keys should be rotated every 90 days for high-impact systems and annually for others. They should be kept in hardware-backed or isolated storage, and high-impact systems should do their signing in isolated environments. The audience claim should be mandatory, and tokens should never be written to logs. The report cites the 2020 SAML-forgery supply-chain attack, and the incident in which forged tokens exposed more than 60,000 government emails, as the failures it is designed to prevent. It is voluntary and aimed at federal agencies, cloud providers and cloud buyers, which makes it most useful as a procurement and architecture checklist. It lands in a week when the top story turned on a long-lived, over-privileged API key stored in source code, and identity infrastructure such as Cisco ISE was under attack. Long lifetimes, keys that never rotate and tokens left in logs are common, and each is easy to measure.

_threatfeed.source_name: CISA; NIST; Infosecurity Magazine

items.title: HHS settles with Ambry Genetics for $700,000 over a 2020 phishing breach — and the findings are about risk analysis, leavers and shared accounts, not the phishing email
items.content_text: The US Department of Health and Human Services’ Office for Civil Rights has settled with Ambry Genetics, a genetic testing laboratory in Aliso Viejo, California, for $700,000 and a two-year corrective action plan. The case dates from January 2020, when a phishing attack compromised an employee email account between 22 and 24 January. It exposed data on 225,370 people, including Social Security or driver’s licence numbers, financial information, diagnoses, lab results, medications and treatment details. OCR’s findings are not about the phishing email itself. They cite the lack of an accurate and thorough risk analysis, the lack of procedures for ending workforce access to electronic health information, and the lack of unique user identification. OCR Director Paula M. Stannard said email phishing “can lead to a breach of PHI and reveal HIPAA Security Rule deficiencies.” HIPAA Journal reports that Ambry also settled the related class action for $12.25 million. The lesson reaches beyond healthcare. Six years after the breach, the regulator is asking about three basic controls: a documented risk analysis, a leaver process and named accounts. Any regulated organisation should be able to show all three on request.

_threatfeed.source_name: HHS Office for Civil Rights; HIPAA Journal

items.title: CISA will stop its weekly vulnerability summary after 28 September and point everyone to KEV — check what quietly depends on the old feed
items.content_text: CISA announced on 17 September that it will stop publishing its weekly Vulnerability Summary bulletin after 28 September 2026. The bulletin is the roundup of newly published CVEs with CVSS scores and patch information. CISA is pointing users to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, alerts and advisories instead. The change follows Binding Operational Directive 26-04, issued in June, which directs federal agencies to prioritise remediation by evidence of exploitation and exposure rather than by CVSS alone, with KEV entries first. For most enterprises the bulletin was not the main feed, because scanners and vendor advisories carry the same data. But it is built into more processes than people realise: weekly patch-review meetings, small-team runbooks, managed-service reports and compliance evidence often cite it by name. The substance of the change is sound, and it matches how this page ranks items: an exploited CVSS 7.8 kernel flaw in KEV deserves faster action than an unexploited 9.8. The job now is to make sure nothing quietly stops working when the feed ends.

_threatfeed.source_name: CISA; SecurityWeek; Cybersecurity Dive; Dark Reading

items.title: The FBI published its first-ever standalone cyber strategy, setting out a shift toward proactive disruption of threat actors rather than investigation after the fact
items.content_text: The FBI released its first dedicated cyber strategy document on 10 September, signalling a move toward proactive disruption operations against threat actors rather than purely reactive investigation. The direction is consistent with recent activity rather than a departure from it — the Xinbi Guarantee action earlier this week, in which the Department of Justice and Treasury seized Telegram channels and cryptocurrency wallets, froze $52.8 million in proceeds from pig-butchering and romance scams and disrupted 13 physical scam compounds, is the kind of operation the strategy describes. This is a policy item with no immediate technical action attached, carried because the operating model it describes changes what a victim organisation can reasonably expect. Disruption operations depend on evidence and telemetry arriving from the private sector early enough to be useful, which puts more weight on the decision to report and on the state of your logs at the moment you make it.

_threatfeed.source_name: FBI; Infosecurity Magazine; Cybersecurity Dive

items.title: The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting duty is now live — 24 hours to notify an actively exploited vulnerability in anything you sell with software in it
items.content_text: The incident-reporting provisions of the EU Cyber Resilience Act took effect this week. Manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must now notify serious security incidents and actively exploited vulnerabilities within a 24-hour window. The obligation lands on a wider population than most organisations assume, because it follows the product rather than the sector: if your company sells anything containing software or connectivity into the EU — equipment, appliances, connected devices, embedded components, packaged software — you are a manufacturer for these purposes, whatever the rest of the business does. Twenty-four hours is short enough that it cannot be met by a process invented after the fact. It has to be decided in advance who declares, on what evidence, and to which authority, and the answer has to work at 6pm on a Friday. The practical difficulty is rarely the notification form; it is the ambiguity in the middle of an incident, when you know something is being exploited but not yet how widely, and the clock has already started.

_threatfeed.source_name: European Commission; Dark Reading; Infosecurity Magazine
_threatfeed.date_note: Reported 11 Sep 2026; reporting requirements effective this week
